title: Recalibrating Africa’s green hydrogen strategy, Part 5
body:
Green hydrogen (H₂) is increasingly framed as Africa’s next industrial frontier.

In Policy Insights N26-2026, I argued that Africa's greatest H₂-led industrial opportunity is not just exporting H₂ molecules or derivatives; it lies in embedding African countries into the manufacturing value chain of H₂ technologies.

While exciting, the short to medium term goal shouldn't be to localize the entire H₂ tech stack at once. That instinct is understandable. It is also strategically dangerous.

The H₂ value chain is an ecosystem of highly different technological segments, each with its own barriers to entry.

Frontier areas like electrolysers, advanced membranes, catalysts, and power electronics are capital-intensive, IP-heavy, and dominated by firms with decades of R&D and consolidated supply chains.

- Entering these segments immediately is neither realistic nor necessary. They require cumulative technological capabilities, long research cycles, and large domestic markets to amortize risk.
- History shows what happens if otherwise: announcement-driven industrialization that struggles to materialize.

Hypothesis 1: African countries are more likely to miss out in a H₂ tech value chain not because they move too slowly; but because they try to do everything at once.

The H₂ tech value chain contains multiple segments that are far more accessible in early industrialization stages:

Balance-of-plant components

Storage systems and tanks

Steel structures and mounting systems

Pipes, valves, and fittings

Compression and transport infrastructure

Assembly, installation, operations, and maintenance

These segments may not headline investment brochures but they are industrially powerful.

- They generate skilled jobs, learning-by-doing, supplier development, and industrial spillovers—without requiring frontier R&D from day one.
- They build on capabilities many African economies already have: fabrication, welding, engineering, mechanical assembly, and industrial services.

Hypothesis 2: A selective, capability-aligned entry strategy anchored in what African countries can realistically produce today and upgrade tomorrow builds credibility with investors and partners, while creating a platform for deeper manufacturing over time.

**Bottom line:** Africa doesn’t need to manufacture everything in the H₂ tech value chain.

Successful late industrializers rarely began at the technological frontier. They entered where capability gaps were manageable, built domestic supplier networks, accumulated tacit knowledge through learning-by-doing, and only later moved upstream.

Selective entry in H₂ tech value chain is therefore not a concession. It is a sequencing strategy.

The question is not whether Africa can manufacture H₂ technologies; it is which parts, when, and under what industrial logic.
